summary: Find the least ship capacity that delivers all packages in order within D days.
mainInsight: Feasibility is monotone in the capacity: a larger ship never needs more days. Binary search the capacity in [max(weights), sum(weights)], and test each candidate with a greedy simulation that loads packages until the next would overflow.

approaches.name: Binary search on the answer
approaches.summary: Check feasibility with a greedy pass and shrink the range.

commonMistakes: Using `<` vs `<=` incorrectly when starting a new day

promptVariants: Which pattern solves 'smallest capacity so that the shipment finishes in D days'?
What makes binary search applicable here?
options: Binary search on the capacity with a greedy day-count check
Sliding window over the package weights in their order
A max-heap of the heaviest packages for each day
Prefix sums with a hash map of the running totals
cards.answer: Binary search on the capacity with a greedy day-count check
cards.explanation: Feasible capacities form a suffix: if C works, C + 1 works.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Sliding window over the package weights: The ship's capacity is not a window length.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Prefix sums with a hash map of the runni: That finds subarrays with an exact sum.

promptVariants: What are the correct bounds for the capacity search and why?
Why is max(weights) the lower bound?
cards.answer: The lower bound is max(weights) because every package must fit on the ship; the upper bound is sum(weights), which ships everything in one day. Between them feasibility is monotone, so binary search finds the minimum feasible capacity.
cards.explanation: Using lo = 1 would test impossible capacities.
Each check is O(n); the capacity range has size about sum(weights), so log S iterations.

promptVariants: Complete the statement: Space complexity (excluding the input): ___
What happens if the lower bound is set to 1 instead of max(weights)?
Which capacities must the check reject?
options: Capacities below the heaviest package are never feasible, so the check must treat them as failures
Nothing changes; the greedy check handles tiny capacities
The search stops being monotone and may loop forever
The answer always becomes sum(weights) in that case
cards.answer: Capacities below the heaviest package are never feasible, so the check must treat them as failures
cards.explanation: Without the bound, a package heavier than C could be 'loaded' by the simple counter and give a wrong day count.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Nothing changes; the greedy check handle: A heavy package would be loaded onto a too-small ship.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The search stops being monotone and may: It stays monotone; it may just return a wrong value.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The answer always becomes sum(weights) i: That is only the upper bound.
